The intelligent design argument is the biological-scale version of the design inference engaged at cosmological scale in §5.1.5. Its proponents, Behe [@behe1996; @behe2007], Dembski [@dembski1998; @dembski2002], Meyer [@meyer2009; @meyer2013], and Plantinga[@plantinga2011, ch. 9] at selective points, argue that biological complexity exhibits features (irreducible complexity, specified complexity, information content) that no unguided process can produce, and that the inference to a designer is the best explanation of those features. The Discovery Institute has carried the position into legal and pedagogical fora, and the *Kitzmiller v. Dover* (2005) decision rendered its legal status in the United States, but the underlying philosophical structure is what concerns the present argument.

ID is not simply fine-tuning at biological scale. Its core commitment is the forward design inference from specified or irreducible biological complexity to intelligent agency. Some religious deployments add special creation, an initially perfect order, or Fall-based explanations of dysteleology, but these are not commitments of ID as such and should be treated as optional extensions rather than the defining package. The Fall-based extension is what makes the religiously extended package self-sealing in a way fine-tuning is not. Fine-tuning claims forward tuning of constants and faces straightforward probabilistic and structural rebuttals. ID has a built-in absorber for every poor-design rebuttal: the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the human spine, the ichneumon wasp, the long catalogue of biological inefficiencies and cruelties[^dysteleology-catalogue]: these are read not as evidence against design but as evidence of *fall from* design. The argument flips dysteleology into confirmation. The present reply engages the core inference and both extensions, not just the core.

*First.* Against the design inference, the present reply draws on the four probability–modality couplings developed at §5.1.5, named here for ease of reference: the standard-side dilemma (a tuner needs a standard, contingent or necessary, and both options foreclose the tuning), the consciousness self-application (the designer cannot be exempted from the constraints that motivated the inference), the modal-structure mask (improbability claims at the structural level are modal questions disguised as probability questions), and the resolution bound (modal-map coarseness inflates apparent contingency). Where §5.1.5 reads "constants" the argument reads "biological configurations." Where it reads "tuning," it reads "designing." The transfer is not automatic, because the two scales do not pose the improbability in the same key. Cosmological fine-tuning is a claim about the modal status of the constants, whether they could have been otherwise. Biological improbability is pressed as something nearer a first-order probability over a space of chemical and genetic configurations, and that is where the argument's intuitive force actually sits.

The biological case cannot be closed merely by transferring the cosmological objections. It turns on empirical models of mutation, selection, drift, developmental constraint, and the causal history of particular systems. Modal and probability questions still matter, but the decisive comparison is whether evolutionary mechanisms or design better explain the evidence under defensible likelihoods.

A further pressure bears on the inference from within its own founding image. Paley's[@paley1802] watch is recognized as designed only against a backdrop that is not: the artifact stands out because the heath it lies on does not bear the same marks. The design inference is therefore contrastive at its root, reading "designed" off a difference between the worked object and the unworked ground. The theistic use of the inference then extends the verdict to everything, the watch and the heath alike, since the same designer is said to have made the ground the watch rests on no less than the watch. But that extension consumes the contrast that licensed the first step: if the ground is designed too, there is no unworked backdrop left against which the watch's design could register, and "designed" stops marking any detectable difference. The inference cannot both earn its conclusion locally (this object, unlike its surroundings, is designed) and generalize that conclusion globally (the surroundings are designed as well) without dissolving the very contrast that gave the local reading its content. Universalized design is indistinguishable from no design at all: not because nothing is designed, but because the predicate has lost the difference it was introduced to track.

The analogy that anchors the inference also marks where it fails. A watch cannot produce another watch, and it is that incapacity, not the watch's intricacy alone, that makes an external maker feel mandatory: nothing about a watch could bring a second watch about. Living things have exactly the capacity the artifact lacks. They reproduce, vary, and are filtered, so the inference cannot be carried from the watch to the organism without importing the watch's sterility as a silent premise, which is to assume rather than show that life, like a watch, could not have come about unaided. The point can be put as a controlled comparison. A kennel holds a hundred dogs. In the first case a breeder selects two of them whose cross yields an animal well suited to a particular hunt: the mating is intended and the result is designed. In the second case the same two dogs are simply the last pair left together and breed as dogs do, with no one intending anything: the litter is identical to the breeder's. Set the two animals side by side. Nothing in either records which history produced it. One was designed and one was not, and the designed one carries no mark of the fact. What the comparison demonstrates is that agency is the sole variable differentiating the two cases; all product-level features are held constant. That result grounds a general claim about the domain the design inference operates in. Design is a prospective process: the designer models a function and selects for it. Selection is a retrospective process: the environment tests against function and retains what fits. Both are function-tracking processes; they differ only in whether the specification precedes or follows the production. For any functional product a designer can yield — any product whose distinguishing features consist in fitness to a function — a sufficiently calibrated selective filter operating on that same function can yield the same, because the features the designer specified-for are precisely the features selection retains. Functional similarity alone may underdetermine whether a trait was designed or selected, because different histories can converge on similar products. But causal histories can leave traces in genealogy, constraint, redundancy, and error-patterns. The design inference must therefore compare full historical models rather than assume either that function uniquely reveals agency or that products can never contain evidence of their origin.

This closes the appeal to specified complexity. A specification is a function-profile: the set of functional properties an object must instantiate to serve its purpose. Selection is differential reproduction based on fitness to the environment. Fitness to the environment is a function-profile. Selection can cumulatively retain variants that function better in a given environment, but it is not literally intentional specification: fitness landscapes emerge from organism–environment relations rather than from a prior semantic target. Dembski's design filter claims to detect specifications that are improbable given chance but probable given design; they are equally probable given cumulative selection operating on the same function-specification — which is the core of the cumulative-selection reply Sober develops.[@sober2008] A specification reliably hit by selection is not a signature of design; it is the predictable output of any process, intentional or not, that tracks function over sufficient iterations. The inference therefore requires a premise that rules out functional-equivalent selection, and that premise cannot be established by examining the product — only by examining the causal history the product-level evidence is being used to infer.

The empirical critique of ID's specific apparatus, Behe's irreducible complexity, Dembski's design filter, Meyer's information argument, lives in evolutionary biology and is not the structural argument's burden; that work has been done there, notably by Sober.[@sober2008] One strand of Behe's case is not purely empirical, however. The *Edge of Evolution* claim (that specified biological information is a quantity the unguided process can generate only within narrow limits) is a thesis about what generates structural information, not only about what the biology shows; the structural reply to it, how the immanent operators of change, composition, and constraint generate form rather than merely presuppose it, is developed where the operators are (Chapter 7), and the information-theoretic features are taken up at §4.3. The couplings at §5.1.5 and the comparative-history burden above bear on the design inference here, however that generative question is settled. The present argument shows what the inference must establish before it runs; the biological literature contests the empirical premises themselves.

*Second.* A historical Fall narrative posits an earlier condition within temporal history from which later corruption proceeds. It need not posit a moment outside T or a categorial origin of time. The relevant objections are empirical and theological—whether there was such an initial condition, what changed, and whether it explains the evidence—not Parasitic Negation alone. There is no moment-prior-to-T from which the first change departed, no temporal position at which "perfect creation" was instantiated as an initial condition outside the order it would initiate (§§2.6.6, 7.2.2, 7.6). The quantitative question of how far back along the dimension the passage runs (whether the past is chronometrically finite or infinite) is a separate question within T, engaged at §5.1.2 against the Kalām's traversal and BGV arguments. The fall narrative in its privileged-t₀ form needs the categorial t₀; the Kalām presses the quantitative question. The two are dispatched at different sections by different machinery. Parasitic Negation applied to T (§§2.1.5, 2.6.6) is the move ID's privileged-t₀ commitment cannot survive: any beginning would already instantiate the order it claims to begin. The question "when did time begin?" admits two readings. The quantitative reading (how far back does succession run) has a numerical answer within whatever cycle one is asking from. The categorial reading (what moment yielded T) is malformed: a moment is what T provides, not what produces T. A moment of perfect creation followed by decay is structurally describable as an event within time. Its difficulty is that ID evidence does not establish such a moment and the biological and cosmological records may count against particular versions of it. The categorial closure dispatches the fall narrative's t₀; it does not dispatch the Kalām's quantitative question, which is the work of §5.1.2.

*Third.* The asymmetric decay vector, the third commitment, reads observed imperfection as evidence of fall from initial perfection. The reading conflates two distinct phenomena: entropy increase (a structural feature of T running) and moral or teleological decline (a normative feature attributed to history). The conflation is what gives the fall claim its empirical footing: every ad hoc construction, vestige, inefficiency, and cruelty in the biological record is reabsorbed as evidence of a perfect prior state from which the present has departed. Entropy increase should not be identified without argument either with moral decline or with Temporality itself. Thermodynamic arrows depend on physical laws and boundary conditions; a Fall theology that links them to corruption owes an additional empirical and doctrinal account. Reading entropy as moral-teleological decline imports a normative direction the present account locates nowhere. T running is not T falling. The fall reading also lacks a historical anchor. It requires a moment at which a first human moral agent acted in a way that initiated decay, but roughly half a billion years of metazoan suffering predate any organism that could be such an agent, and contemporary population genetics rules out descent of *Homo sapiens* from a single founding pair within the span the lineage permits.[@venemaMcknight2017] Plantinga's *O Felix Culpa*[@plantinga2004] relocates the fall into a privileged theological moment whose empirical anchorage is set aside; the move preserves the theological structure at the cost of giving up exactly the historical fall the original argument needs. Without the entropy-as-fall reading, and without a historical fall to anchor it, the dysteleology cases revert to what they were before being absorbed by the theodicy: evidence against the design inference, not evidence for it.

A note on scope. The fall claim also makes a directional empirical prediction (that observed history runs away from an initial perfection), and there are aggregate gradients in human social life and in religious demand that appear to run the other way. Those gradients are contested empirical terrain, and the present section does not rest on them: the fall narrative is already foreclosed structurally, by the categorial-t₀ argument and the entropy misreading above, whatever the long-run social data ultimately show. The substantive case that these gradients positively confirm the structural account is made where that work belongs (§8.12.4 on the moral arc and §8.14.4 on declining religiosity) and is left to stand or fall there on its own evidence.

*What closes.* The core inference and its two extensions dispatch separately, and the package does not survive their separation. The design inference carries the couplings at §5.1.5 and the comparative-history burden developed above. The privileged origin moment is foreclosed by the present argument that T has no exterior or prior origin moment, a categorial closure that leaves the quantitative question of a finite chronometric past to §5.1.2 and Chapter 7. The asymmetric decay vector misreads entropy as moral decline. A Fall-based absorber can make a religious design theory resistant to dysteleological evidence, but it is an optional theological auxiliary rather than part of ID's core. It incurs empirical and explanatory burdens concerning the initial condition, mechanism, and scope of corruption. Without the absorber, the design inference at biological scale inherits the burdens of the design inference at cosmological scale, which §5.1.5 leaves undischarged.

[[1]](dysteleology-catalogue): The catalogue extends to reproduction itself. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists estimates that as many as one in four recognized pregnancies ends in miscarriage (ACOG estimate, cited in Deshpande and Kucirka, *StatPearls*, 2023), and a substantial further share of fertilized eggs are lost before implantation is ever detected. A designer credited with intending the birth of every child inherits, on the same accounting, a design in which a large fraction of attempts at that outcome fail before term.
